source.title: Use of direct oral anticoagulants in patients with obesity for treatment and prevention of venous thromboembolism: Updated communication from the ISTH SSC Subcommittee on Control of Anticoagulation

extraction_metadata.scope_note: This source is a secondary ISTH SSC guidance communication, not a primary empirical study. Quantitative findings from cited studies are represented as the communication's secondary reports and tagged secondary_reported_result. Bibliographic entries are not atomized.

atoms.canonical_statement: The ISTH SSC communication reviewed available DOAC evidence in obesity and bariatric surgery and issued updated guidance for VTE treatment and prevention.
The authors searched PubMed for DOAC, obesity, VTE treatment or prevention, bariatric surgery, and PK/PD or drug-level evidence through August 1, 2020.
All authors held multiple video-conference discussions to review the evidence and reach consensus recommendations.
The review and guidance were limited to venous thromboembolism and did not address atrial fibrillation as a treatment population.

The treatment evidence in obesity consisted of phase 3 analyses, phase 4 observational studies and claims comparisons, and systematic reviews or meta-analyses, with heterogeneous weight definitions and comparators.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 3.1 Clinical data for VTE treatment

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that, in a US claims analysis of morbidly obese patients, apixaban was associated with lower recurrent VTE risk than warfarin, HR 0.63 with 95% CI 0.52 to 0.78.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients in US insurance claims analysis summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that, in the same US claims analysis, apixaban was associated with lower major bleeding risk than warfarin, HR 0.70 with 95% CI 0.56 to 0.89.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients in US insurance claims analysis summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that the EINSTEIN DVT/PE obesity subgroup had no statistically clear difference in recurrent VTE at 12 months with rivaroxaban versus warfarin, HR 1.45 with 95% CI 0.62 to 3.39.

population.label: EINSTEIN DVT/PE participants with BMI at least 35 kg/m2

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports no statistically clear difference in major bleeding in the EINSTEIN DVT/PE obesity subgroup with rivaroxaban versus warfarin, HR 0.71 with 95% CI 0.22 to 2.24.

population.label: EINSTEIN DVT/PE participants with BMI at least 35 kg/m2 assessed for major bleeding

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that a propensity-matched electronic health record study in patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 found lower recurrent VTE risk with rivaroxaban versus warfarin at 12 months, HR 0.63 with 95% CI 0.54 to 0.74.

population.label: Patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 in propensity-matched EHR study summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that the same EHR study found no clear difference in major bleeding at 12 months with rivaroxaban versus warfarin, HR 1.00 with 95% CI 0.73 to 1.36.

population.label: Patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 in propensity-matched EHR study summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that a meta-analysis of more than 6500 patients with extreme obesity found similar recurrent VTE with pooled DOACs versus warfarin, OR 1.07 with 95% CI 0.93 to 1.23.

population.label: Patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 or weight over 120 kg in five-study meta-analysis summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that the same extreme-obesity meta-analysis found a nonsignificant trend toward less major bleeding with pooled DOACs versus warfarin, OR 0.80 with 95% CI 0.54 to 1.17.

population.label: Patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 or weight over 120 kg in five-study meta-analysis summarized by the communication

atoms.canonical_statement: The review found no VTE treatment studies that analyzed betrixaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban individually in obesity.
Across pooled DOAC observational studies, the communication summarizes efficacy and safety as similar to VKA or similar across body-weight categories.
The source judged evidence insufficient to guide reduced-dose DOAC use for severely obese patients after the first 6 months of full-dose extended VTE treatment.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 3.1.5 Dose reduction for extended VTE treatment

atoms.canonical_statement: The VTE prevention evidence reviewed by the communication came primarily from orthopedic thromboprophylaxis studies.

source_anchor.paragraph: Section 3.2 Clinical data for VTE prevention

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that pooled ADVANCE-2 and ADVANCE-3 data in participants with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 showed similar primary VTE outcomes with apixaban versus enoxaparin, RR 0.52 with 95% CI 0.25 to 1.07.

population.label: ADVANCE-2 and ADVANCE-3 participants with BMI at least 30 kg/m2

concept.text: Proximal DVT, nonfatal PE, or VTE-related death

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that pooled dabigatran orthopedic prophylaxis data in patients with BMI at least 35 kg/m2 showed similar VTE and VTE-related mortality versus enoxaparin, OR 1.25 with 95% CI 0.33 to 4.75.

population.label: Orthopedic surgery participants with BMI at least 35 kg/m2 in pooled dabigatran phase 3 analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that pooled RECORD trials in patients weighing more than 90 kg showed similar symptomatic VTE and all-cause mortality with rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin, HR 0.49 with 95% CI 0.20 to 1.10.

population.label: RECORD trial participants weighing more than 90 kg

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports more major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding with rivaroxaban versus enoxaparin in the pooled RECORD analysis, 4.4% versus 2.7%, HR 1.6 with 95% CI 1.1 to 2.4.

population.label: RECORD trial participants weighing more than 90 kg

concept.text: Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding

atoms.canonical_statement: The review identified no betrixaban VTE prevention data analyzed by body weight.

The communication reports that a five-trial meta-analysis in postarthroplasty patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 found similar VTE or VTE-related death with apixaban or dabigatran versus enoxaparin, OR 0.88 with 95% CI 0.32 to 2.37.

population.label: Postarthroplasty patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 in five phase 3 RCT meta-analysis

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that the same postarthroplasty meta-analysis found similar major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding with apixaban or dabigatran versus enoxaparin, OR 0.67 with 95% CI 0.35 to 1.28.

population.label: Postarthroplasty patients with BMI at least 30 kg/m2 in five phase 3 RCT meta-analysis

concept.text: Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that healthy subjects weighing at least 120 kg had a lower mean peak apixaban concentration than the 65 to 85 kg reference group, 144 versus 207 ng/mL, along with 23% lower AUC.

population.label: Healthy subjects in three body-weight categories

outcome.measurement_method: Plasma concentration after a single apixaban dose

quantitative_result.effect_measure: mean peak concentration in high-weight group

atoms.canonical_statement: The communication reports that, in a 100-patient high-weight cohort, all 19 apixaban peak levels and 89% of 18 trough levels were within expected ranges.

The communication reports that 20% of 10 dabigatran-treated patients weighing more than 120 kg had peak concentrations below the usual on-treatment range and below the median trough level reported in the literature.
The communication reports that one rivaroxaban study found 28% of 21 patients over 120 kg had peak levels below the fifth percentile of usual on-treatment concentrations.
The communication reports that another high-weight cohort had 45% of 58 rivaroxaban peak levels below expected ranges, while all 21 trough levels were within expected ranges.

The PK/PD synthesis judged body weight to have little overall effect on rivaroxaban PK/PD, found obesity-related PK changes for apixaban but mostly expected measured levels, and considered dabigatran data limited with a concerning proportion of low levels.

The source states that DOAC therapeutic targets are unknown, expected or on-therapy ranges are not validated therapeutic ranges, and interpatient and intrapatient variability limits interpretation of measured levels.
Supplemental Table 1 summarizes apixaban as having lower peak levels with increasing body weight and lower AUC or no change in studies of BMI above 40 kg/m2.
Supplemental Table 1 summarizes dabigatran as having lower peak levels with increasing body weight and no available BMI above 40 kg/m2 drug-level data.
Supplemental Table 1 lists no available increasing-body-weight or BMI above 40 kg/m2 drug-level data for edoxaban.
Supplemental Table 1 summarizes rivaroxaban studies as showing either no change or lower peak levels with increasing body weight and no available BMI above 40 kg/m2 drug-level data in the table.

The source describes apixaban absorption as primarily upper gastrointestinal, with Roux-en-Y gastric bypass possibly reducing absorption while gastric banding and sleeve gastrectomy are expected to be less disruptive.
The source describes dabigatran absorption as lower stomach and proximal small intestine and lists possible reduced absorption after gastric banding, sleeve gastrectomy, and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.
The source describes edoxaban absorption as proximal small intestine and acid dependent and lists possible reduced absorption after gastric banding, sleeve gastrectomy, and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.
The source describes rivaroxaban absorption as largely gastric and lists possible reduced absorption after gastric banding, sleeve gastrectomy, and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.
The communication reports that a post-bariatric-surgery drug-level study found a lower median peak rivaroxaban concentration than controls, 159 versus 249 ng/mL, p = 0.02.

population.label: Patients on chronic anticoagulation after bariatric surgery and control participants in study summarized by the communication

quantitative_result.effect_measure: median peak concentration in bariatric-surgery group

atoms.canonical_statement: The same post-bariatric-surgery study summarized by the communication found apixaban peak plasma levels within the expected range.

In the bariatric-surgery discussion, the authors state that DOACs may be appropriate after at least 6 to 12 months, while favoring parenteral anticoagulation in the early or acute setting and considering a trough level after a later switch to a DOAC.
The source identifies sparse evidence at the highest weights, especially BMI at least 50 kg/m2 and weight above 150 kg.
The evidence base used inconsistent comparisons, with some studies comparing DOACs with VKA and others comparing a drug across weight categories.
The source notes that individual DOAC data are limited and should not be assumed interchangeable across the drug class.
The authors state that no DOAC has a clinically validated therapeutic range for VTE prophylaxis or treatment and that PK/PD data cannot replace clinical outcome evidence.
The authors identify the absence of adequately powered prospective randomized trials in severe obesity as the main evidence limitation and call current conclusions preliminary.
The formal guidance concludes that any DOAC is appropriate for patients with BMI up to 40 kg/m2 or weight up to 120 kg.

For VTE treatment above BMI 40 kg/m2 or weight 120 kg, the formal guidance suggests standard-dose rivaroxaban or apixaban as appropriate options, with fewer supportive data for apixaban than rivaroxaban.
For primary VTE prevention, the formal guidance suggests standard-dose rivaroxaban or apixaban as appropriate options regardless of high BMI and weight within approved prophylaxis indications.

The formal guidance suggests not using dabigatran, edoxaban, or betrixaban for VTE treatment or prevention when BMI is above 40 kg/m2 or weight is above 120 kg because the supporting evidence was unconvincing or absent.
The formal guidance suggests not routinely monitoring peak or trough drug-specific DOAC levels because the available data were insufficient to guide management decisions.

After bariatric surgery, the formal guidance suggests avoiding DOACs in the acute setting, using parenteral anticoagulation initially, and considering VKA or a DOAC after at least 4 weeks of parenteral treatment; if a DOAC is chosen, it suggests a trough level to assess absorption and bioavailability.
The authors conclude that the available evidence supports rivaroxaban and apixaban as potentially adequate VTE treatment options in obesity regardless of body weight and BMI.

The authors conclude that plasma DOAC levels within published expected ranges may reassure clinicians but are insufficient to direct management because therapeutic target values have not been linked to clinical outcomes.
The authors call for randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity, especially extreme obesity, because clinical evidence remains limited.

The conflict-of-interest section reports Janssen Scientific Affairs funding for Martin, grants or fees involving several anticoagulant manufacturers for Huisman and Beyer-Westendorf, Bristol-Myers-Squibb consulting fees for Moll, and no conflicts for Davidson and Sandset.
